snippet.text:
The increasing per capita share of vegetarian and vegan foods and the growing nutritional awareness of various consumer groups are driving the global nut market. In recent years, production of almost all nut species across the world has expanded. The selected studies on nut trees include almond (Prunus dulcis (Miller) D.A. Webb), hazelnut (Corylus avellana L.), pecan (Carya illinoinensis (Wangenh.) C. Koch), pistachio (Pistacia vera L.), and walnut (Juglans regia L.). The latest reports point to a global area of 5.3 million hectares under nut tree cultivation, excluding pecans. With around 43% of the area and 42% of the production, almonds are by far the most important crop (FAOSTAT 2023). Pecan trees are native to North America; Mexico and the United States of America (USA) lead world production. South Africa, China and Brazil continue to gradually increase their production. The global harvested area of almond trees has expanded significantly for various reasons, including the mechanization of harvesting; a significant increase in global demand, which has led to a gradual increase in the prices paid to growers, the introduction of new self-fertile cultivars with late or extra-late flowering, which reduce the risk of production losses due to spring frosts; and worldwire awareness of the health benefits of nuts (Mirás-Avalos et al. 2023). Because almond trees have low chilling requirements, vegetative development and flowering begin much earlier in the season than in other deciduous tree species; therefore, to minimize cold damage, plant breeders are striving to develop cultivars that flower later. Rootstocks are available for most tree nut species except hazelnuts. 

Studies on almond nuts predominate (Table 7), although there is ample information on the other species. The studies were mainly conducted in semi-arid areas in 11 countries with a temperate Mediterranean climate, including Spain, Australia, the USA, Portugal, France, Serbia, Chile, Turkey and South Africa. This extensive geographic distribution of the selected studies   offers various perspectives that favour the analysis of the appropriate standard K c and K cb values for all the crops.

attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of agronomic factors that help explain why almonds occupy roughly 700,000 hectares—about 31% of global tree nut harvested area—disproportionate to other tree nuts. Where relevant, we contrast almonds with major comparators (walnuts, pistachios, hazelnuts/chestnuts) and anchor each claim in evidence.

1) Climate adaptability and phenology: heat tolerance and flexible chilling needs
- Almonds have supported widespread cultivation across Mediterranean climates and are now a global crop spanning hundreds of thousands of hectares, benefiting from systems that intensify production on existing land with efficient input use and mechanization supported by rootstocks that control growth and enable narrow-row, high-density canopies <cite id="e7009f37-0">The almond tree accounts for 31% of total nut crop production with 700,000 ha and new systems emphasize rootstocks enabling intensification for efficiency in labor and mechanization under sustainability intensification pathways</cite>. 
- Modern intensive almond orchards select early-blooming, self-incompatible cultivars that rely on cross-pollination and, increasingly, on self-compatible varieties and dwarfing rootstocks that promote earlier, more efficient fruiting and higher planting densities, enabling greater area expansion per unit land <cite id="e7009f37-2">Almond production is dominated by a few commercial varieties, often self-incompatible and early-blooming for cross-pollination; dwarfing rootstocks enable higher densities while improving tolerance to chlorosis and pests</cite>. 
- Comparative evidence shows pistachio cultivation can succeed in cold-winter regions when chilling units exceed a threshold (~800–1000 hours ≤7.2 °C for ‘Kerman’), indicating broader chilling-niche tolerance than many temperate tree nuts and reinforcing the idea that almonds’ flexible phenology and irrigation-enabled cropping windows allow expansion into arid and semi-arid zones <cite id="ca57f832-0">Pistachio dormancy requires ~800–1000 chilling hours at ≤7.2 °C, and surveyed sites in Spain met or exceeded these requirements</cite>. 
- In contrast, walnuts are among the “Big Five” tree nuts but have different market-share dynamics; almonds and walnuts lead production (31% and 21%, respectively), implying distinct agronomic niches where walnut’s climatic and canopy-management demands differ from almond’s intensifiable systems <cite id="fcb52f08-0">Global nut production growth has elevated the “Big Five”; almonds (31%) and walnuts (21%) lead production, with cashews (17%), pistachios (14%), and hazelnuts (12%) following</cite>. 
- Water productivity also favors tree nuts over field crops; almonds, pistachios, hazelnuts, and walnuts fall in the same order of water footprint per gram of protein as red meat, and pistachios are among the highest per gram without irrigation, which elevates the economic and agronomic value of efficient irrigation systems in almonds <cite id="fcb52f08-3">Almonds (65.4 L/kg) and pistachios (103.9 L/g) show relatively high water footprints per gram, comparable to red meat in protein-normalized terms, highlighting the premium placed on efficient irrigation and management</cite>.

2) Irrigation dependence and water-use efficiency: arid-zone expansion enabled by drip and scheduling
- Almonds are highly sensitive to water stress, especially during reproductive and early fruit development under high evaporative demand; sustainable productivity hinges on precise irrigation scheduling (low-to-moderate deficit irrigation) to meet peak needs without compromising kernel fill or shatter, a management niche where drip irrigation and remote sensing-based scheduling have been deployed at scale <cite id="e7009f37-2">Despite drought resistance, almond trees have poor salt stress tolerance; prolonged water scarcity during fruit development under high evaporative demand severely compromises yields, making low-deficit irrigation essential during peak water needs</cite>. 
- In paired almond–pistachio systems using drip irrigation, seasonal applied water averaged 898 mm for almonds vs 763 mm for pistachio, with weekly irrigation hours ramping through the season and a 14–13 day preharvest dry-down—illustrating intensive, metered water use that is economically viable where water infrastructure exists <cite id="ca57f832-2">Almond and pistachio orchards received 898 mm and 762.5 mm of applied water, respectively; almonds were irrigated 2–70 hours/week, dried 14 days preharvest; pistachio irrigation was 5–50 hours/week with 13 days drying before early October harvest</cite>. 
- Water productivity comparisons show many tree nuts have higher blue-water footprints per gram than pistachios, which underscores why almonds—like other tree nuts—compete favorably in water-rich basins (e.g., Central Valley, parts of India/Pakistan) where irrigation efficiency and cost are favorable relative to staple crops <cite id="fcb52f08-3">Pistachios have the largest blue-water footprint per gram (73.8 L/g), with almonds (19.1 L/g) and walnuts (17.1 L/g) similar; relative to groundnuts/chestnuts, tree nuts’ water footprints are much larger, intensifying the importance of irrigation management</cite>. 
- Conversely, some tree nut species exhibit higher rainfall dependence and longer canopies that are less compatible with high-density mechanization, limiting area expansion relative to almonds where dwarfing rootstocks and narrow rows enable earlier cropping and lower labor per hectare <cite id="e7009f37-0">Rootstocks enabling super high-density orchards enhance input efficiency (labor and mechanization) and precocity, a pathway central to almond’s area expansion</cite>.

3) Soil and salinity constraints; nitrogen and micronutrient requirements
- Almonds’ salt-stress tolerance is comparatively poor; salinity during fruit development elevates risk of physiological disorders and yield loss, which increases the attractiveness of orchards with reliable, quality irrigation water and soil management (leaching, gypsum/foliar amendments) relative to other tree nuts with broader salinity tolerance <cite id="e7009f37-2">Despite drought resistance, almonds show poor salt-stress tolerance; prolonged water scarcity with high evaporative demand during fruit development compromises yields</cite>. 
- Intensive systems emphasize balanced irrigation with fertilization to avoid asphyxia/phytotoxicity and chlorosis; dwarfing rootstocks improve tolerance to these stresses and to pests/diseases, supporting higher planting densities and greater area per farm <cite id="e7009f37-2">Dwarfing rootstocks increase tolerance to asphyxia and chlorosis and improve pest/disease resistance, enabling higher planting densities and intensive systems</cite>. 
- Compared with some tree nuts (e.g., chestnuts, groundnuts) that have lower water footprints, almond orchards require deliberate nutrient and water management; this has driven adoption of precision irrigation and soil-health practices that are regionally concentrated and thus contribute to area share where inputs and infrastructure are available <cite id="fcb52f08-3">Chestnuts and groundnuts exhibit lower water footprints per kg/protein than almonds/walnuts/pistachios, indicating different agronomic niches and management emphases</cite>.

4) Pollination biology and cultivar selection: early bloom, cross-compatibility, and orchard design
- Commercial almond varieties are dominated by a small set of self-incompatible, early-blooming cultivars that require cross-pollination; this biology favors orchard design that concentrates bloom and synchronizes pollinator services, and it has driven selection of cultivars and rootstocks optimized for early, uniform cropping and mechanical harvest windows <cite id="e7009f37-2">Most orchards are grafted onto medium-to-high vigor rootstocks at low-to-medium densities, but intensive systems select self-compatible cultivars for effective pollination and dwarfing rootstocks for higher densities</cite>. 
- Rootstock choice is a first-order agronomic lever: growth-controlling dwarfing rootstocks enable “super high-density” systems with narrow rows and compact canopies that mature earlier, increase cropping frequency, and improve labor/mechanization efficiency—key to achieving high area productivity and expansion <cite id="e7009f37-0">Growth-controlling rootstocks enable super high-density systems with narrow rows/canopies, enhancing input efficiency and precocity</cite>. 
- In contrast, walnut and pistachio cultivation often accommodate multivoltine pests over longer, staggered vulnerability windows; management complexity and harvest timing differ, which can slow area expansion relative to almonds when pollination and harvest logistics are streamlined by cultivar/rootstock selection <cite id="ca57f832-3">Navel orangeworm affects California almond, pistachio, and walnut; new crop Nonpareil almonds are vulnerable for 5–8 weeks at harvest, and pistachios have an 8–10 week post-hull-split vulnerability period</cite>. 

5) Pest and disease management: shared risks and integrated control needs
- Almonds, pistachios, and walnuts share the navel orangeworm, a multivoltine moth with aflatoxin-producing fungal associates; this elevates the cost and complexity of season-long monitoring and integrated management, especially during extended preharvest dry-downs when nuts are most vulnerable <cite id="ca57f832-3">Navel orangeworm is primary pest across almond, pistachio, and walnut; monitoring is critical due to phenology-driven vulnerability windows and aflatoxin risk</cite>. 
- In practice, almond and pistachio orchards dry down for 13–14 days prior to harvest to synchronize shuckability; pest/disease risk management is time-sensitive and resource-intensive, but the economic value of high-value nuts supports these inputs and infrastructure, facilitating large-scale adoption in irrigated basins <cite id="ca57f832-2">Almond and pistachio orchards were dried for 14 and 13 days preharvest, respectively, as part of structured irrigation scheduling</cite>. 
- Compared with some other tree nuts, this shared pest complex and the need for tight agronomic scheduling are major drivers of input intensity; however, economies of scale in irrigation, pollination, and pest monitoring have allowed almond area to expand rapidly where markets and infrastructure exist <cite id="ca57f832-3">The combined farm gate value of these crops exceeds $9B in California (>900,000 ha), underscoring strong market and management support despite elevated pest/disease risks</cite>. 

6) Harvest logistics and processing: shorter, synchronized harvest windows and mechanization
- Almond varieties like Nonpareil have a concentrated 5–8 week harvest vulnerability and shuckability window after hull split, enabling synchronized orchard operations and efficient mechanical harvesting—logistics that align well with irrigation-intensive regions capable of rapid, repeated passes for thinning, irrigation control, and shaker-based harvest <cite id="ca57f832-3">Nonpareil almonds become vulnerable at hull split for 5–8 weeks until harvest</cite>. 
- Pistachio systems similarly schedule irrigation and implement 8–10 week vulnerability windows post-hull split, with preharvest drying for early October harvest; these practices illustrate that tree nut expansion depends on agronomic control of moisture and canopy to align with processing and market windows <cite id="ca57f832-2">Pistachio vulnerability follows hull breakdown for eight to ten weeks from mid-August through mid-October with structured irrigation and 13-day drying before harvest</cite>. 
- Orchards that can be dried down and shaken efficiently reduce labor per hectare relative to tree nuts with more fragmented harvest logistics, supporting higher area share when irrigation water and mechanization are available <cite id="ca57f832-2">Preharvest drying schedules and drip irrigation management demonstrate how irrigation timing directly controls harvest logistics</cite>. 

7) Market value and intensification: high value enabling efficient input use
- The global demand for almonds has expanded markedly in the past decade, driven by online channels and perceived health benefits; intensification pathways (precision irrigation, rootstocks, cultivars) convert less land into higher, more stable yields, reinforcing the economic logic of extensive planting where water and capital are available <cite id="e7009f37-2">Global demand growth from e-commerce and nutrition-driven markets has intensified almond cultivation, with intensive systems selecting cultivars and dwarfing rootstocks for higher yields and sustainability</cite>. 
- High-value crops support extensive research and extension to optimize cultivar/rootstock choices, irrigation scheduling, and pest monitoring; in California, >900,000 hectares of almonds, pistachios, and walnuts underpin a multi-billion dollar industry, showing how agronomic precision scales with economic value <cite id="ca57f832-3">California hosts >900,000 ha of almond, pistachio, and walnut with combined farm-gate value >$9B, highlighting the economic pull of high-value nut production</cite>. 

8) Comparative constraints vs other tree nuts
- Chestnuts and groundnuts tend to have lower overall water footprints per kg and protein, indicating agronomic niches where rainfall capture and lower input intensity are feasible, but they also face different processing/logistics and market dynamics that limit area share relative to almonds <cite id="fcb52f08-3">Chestnuts (9.7 L/g) and groundnuts (0.8 L/g) have much lower water footprints than almonds (65.4 L/kg) and others, reflecting different input and irrigation regimes</cite>. 
- Hazelnuts and walnuts often require higher chilling and have longer, staggered vulnerability periods and more complex canopy management; national programs invest in regional adaptation and logistics infrastructure to expand area, suggesting slower conversion to large-scale plantings compared with almonds where rootstock-driven intensification is mature <cite id="fcb52f08-0">Walnut and hazelnut area expansion in Ukraine is supported by associations focused on adaptation to local climatic conditions and logistics, reflecting longer-term, infrastructure-dependent growth</cite>. 
- Almonds also benefit from irrigation basins and export logistics tailored to their kernel traits; in contrast, nuts like pistachios and walnuts face higher aflatoxin risk during extended dry-downs and require robust monitoring, adding to management costs though not deterring area growth where inputs are available <cite id="ca57f832-3">Navel orangeworm and aflatoxin risk complicate almond, pistachio, and walnut management; economic value supports intensive monitoring and control</cite>. 
- Salinity and heat constraints remain a key agronomic boundary for almond expansion; unlike some tree nuts with broader salt tolerance, almond orchards often require water quality management and heat-stress mitigation (e.g., shade/deficit irrigation timing) to sustain yields in arid regions, which steers planting into irrigated corridors rather than dryland zones <cite id="e7009f37-2">Almonds’ poor salt-stress tolerance and sensitivity to high evaporative demand during fruit development drive targeted irrigation management and site selection</cite>. 

9) Synthesis: why almonds’ area share is disproportionate
- Almonds combine flexible but managed phenology, rootstock-enabled intensification, and irrigation-based climate control to deliver high yields per hectare where water and infrastructure exist, producing economies of scale in pollination, pest management, and mechanized harvest that are attractive to growers and investors <cite id="e7009f37-0">Rootstocks enabling super high-density systems improve input efficiency and precocity</cite><cite id="e7009f37-2">Dwarfing rootstocks, cultivar selection, and irrigation scheduling underpin intensive almond production</cite><cite id="ca57f832-2">Paired drip-irrigated almond and pistachio systems illustrate precise, scheduled water use and preharvest drying aligned to harvest</cite>.

Snippet: The navel orangeworm, Amyelois transitella Walker (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae) is the primary pest of California almond (Prunus dulcis; 81% of the world supply), pistachio (Pistacia vera; 67% of the world supply) and walnut (Juglans regia) (Statista 2022, Almonds 2023). Currently these crops are planted in > 900,000 ha in California and have a combined annual farm gate value exceeding US $9 billion (Siegel and Gilcrease 2022). This multivoltine moth has a mutualistic relationship with fungal species belonging to the genus Aspergillus that produce aflatoxins, consequently feeding causes direct damage to the nuts and can cause secondary fungal infection (Palumbo et al. 2014;Ampt et al. 2016;Picot et al. 2017;Bush et al. 2018). 

Monitoring for A. transitella is important because damage in almonds and pistachios results from a complex interplay of crop phenology and pest population dynamics (Wilson et al. 2020). New crop Nonpareil almonds, the most valuable variety, become vulnerable during hull split (late June-July) when the suture widens exposing the shell and/or nut. The period of vulnerability for Nonpareil almonds typically lasts 5 to 8 weeks until the nuts are shaken from the tree at harvest; the other almond varieties mature from late August through October (Haviland et al. 2022a). New crop pistachios are vulnerable when the hull breaks down after the nut ripens, exposing the split shell for eight to ten weeks from mid-August through mid-October (Haviland et al. 2022b).

Below is a synthesis of agronomic factors that help explain why almonds occupy roughly 700,000 hectares—about 31% of global tree nut harvested area—disproportionate to other tree nuts. Where relevant, we contrast almonds with major comparators (walnuts, pistachios, hazelnuts/chestnuts) and anchor each claim in evidence.

1) Climate adaptability and phenology: heat tolerance and flexible chilling needs
- Almonds have supported widespread cultivation across Mediterranean climates and are now a global crop spanning hundreds of thousands of hectares, benefiting from systems that intensify production on existing land with efficient input use and mechanization supported by rootstocks that control growth and enable narrow-row, high-density canopies <cite id="e7009f37-0">The almond tree accounts for 31% of total nut crop production with 700,000 ha and new systems emphasize rootstocks enabling intensification for efficiency in labor and mechanization under sustainability intensification pathways</cite>. 
- Modern intensive almond orchards select early-blooming, self-incompatible cultivars that rely on cross-pollination and, increasingly, on self-compatible varieties and dwarfing rootstocks that promote earlier, more efficient fruiting and higher planting densities, enabling greater area expansion per unit land <cite id="e7009f37-2">Almond production is dominated by a few commercial varieties, often self-incompatible and early-blooming for cross-pollination; dwarfing rootstocks enable higher densities while improving tolerance to chlorosis and pests</cite>. 
- Comparative evidence shows pistachio cultivation can succeed in cold-winter regions when chilling units exceed a threshold (~800–1000 hours ≤7.2 °C for ‘Kerman’), indicating broader chilling-niche tolerance than many temperate tree nuts and reinforcing the idea that almonds’ flexible phenology and irrigation-enabled cropping windows allow expansion into arid and semi-arid zones <cite id="ca57f832-0">Pistachio dormancy requires ~800–1000 chilling hours at ≤7.2 °C, and surveyed sites in Spain met or exceeded these requirements</cite>. 
- In contrast, walnuts are among the “Big Five” tree nuts but have different market-share dynamics; almonds and walnuts lead production (31% and 21%, respectively), implying distinct agronomic niches where walnut’s climatic and canopy-management demands differ from almond’s intensifiable systems <cite id="fcb52f08-0">Global nut production growth has elevated the “Big Five”; almonds (31%) and walnuts (21%) lead production, with cashews (17%), pistachios (14%), and hazelnuts (12%) following</cite>. 
- Water productivity also favors tree nuts over field crops; almonds, pistachios, hazelnuts, and walnuts fall in the same order of water footprint per gram of protein as red meat, and pistachios are among the highest per gram without irrigation, which elevates the economic and agronomic value of efficient irrigation systems in almonds <cite id="fcb52f08-3">Almonds (65.4 L/kg) and pistachios (103.9 L/g) show relatively high water footprints per gram, comparable to red meat in protein-normalized terms, highlighting the premium placed on efficient irrigation and management</cite>.

2) Irrigation dependence and water-use efficiency: arid-zone expansion enabled by drip and scheduling
- Almonds are highly sensitive to water stress, especially during reproductive and early fruit development under high evaporative demand; sustainable productivity hinges on precise irrigation scheduling (low-to-moderate deficit irrigation) to meet peak needs without compromising kernel fill or shatter, a management niche where drip irrigation and remote sensing-based scheduling have been deployed at scale <cite id="e7009f37-2">Despite drought resistance, almond trees have poor salt stress tolerance; prolonged water scarcity during fruit development under high evaporative demand severely compromises yields, making low-deficit irrigation essential during peak water needs</cite>. 
- In paired almond–pistachio systems using drip irrigation, seasonal applied water averaged 898 mm for almonds vs 763 mm for pistachio, with weekly irrigation hours ramping through the season and a 14–13 day preharvest dry-down—illustrating intensive, metered water use that is economically viable where water infrastructure exists <cite id="ca57f832-2">Almond and pistachio orchards received 898 mm and 762.5 mm of applied water, respectively; almonds were irrigated 2–70 hours/week, dried 14 days preharvest; pistachio irrigation was 5–50 hours/week with 13 days drying before early October harvest</cite>. 
- Water productivity comparisons show many tree nuts have higher blue-water footprints per gram than pistachios, which underscores why almonds—like other tree nuts—compete favorably in water-rich basins (e.g., Central Valley, parts of India/Pakistan) where irrigation efficiency and cost are favorable relative to staple crops <cite id="fcb52f08-3">Pistachios have the largest blue-water footprint per gram (73.8 L/g), with almonds (19.1 L/g) and walnuts (17.1 L/g) similar; relative to groundnuts/chestnuts, tree nuts’ water footprints are much larger, intensifying the importance of irrigation management</cite>. 
- Conversely, some tree nut species exhibit higher rainfall dependence and longer canopies that are less compatible with high-density mechanization, limiting area expansion relative to almonds where dwarfing rootstocks and narrow rows enable earlier cropping and lower labor per hectare <cite id="e7009f37-0">Rootstocks enabling super high-density orchards enhance input efficiency (labor and mechanization) and precocity, a pathway central to almond’s area expansion</cite>.

3) Soil and salinity constraints; nitrogen and micronutrient requirements
- Almonds’ salt-stress tolerance is comparatively poor; salinity during fruit development elevates risk of physiological disorders and yield loss, which increases the attractiveness of orchards with reliable, quality irrigation water and soil management (leaching, gypsum/foliar amendments) relative to other tree nuts with broader salinity tolerance <cite id="e7009f37-2">Despite drought resistance, almonds show poor salt-stress tolerance; prolonged water scarcity with high evaporative demand during fruit development compromises yields</cite>. 
- Intensive systems emphasize balanced irrigation with fertilization to avoid asphyxia/phytotoxicity and chlorosis; dwarfing rootstocks improve tolerance to these stresses and to pests/diseases, supporting higher planting densities and greater area per farm <cite id="e7009f37-2">Dwarfing rootstocks increase tolerance to asphyxia and chlorosis and improve pest/disease resistance, enabling higher planting densities and intensive systems</cite>. 
- Compared with some tree nuts (e.g., chestnuts, groundnuts) that have lower water footprints, almond orchards require deliberate nutrient and water management; this has driven adoption of precision irrigation and soil-health practices that are regionally concentrated and thus contribute to area share where inputs and infrastructure are available <cite id="fcb52f08-3">Chestnuts and groundnuts exhibit lower water footprints per kg/protein than almonds/walnuts/pistachios, indicating different agronomic niches and management emphases</cite>.

4) Pollination biology and cultivar selection: early bloom, cross-compatibility, and orchard design
- Commercial almond varieties are dominated by a small set of self-incompatible, early-blooming cultivars that require cross-pollination; this biology favors orchard design that concentrates bloom and synchronizes pollinator services, and it has driven selection of cultivars and rootstocks optimized for early, uniform cropping and mechanical harvest windows <cite id="e7009f37-2">Most orchards are grafted onto medium-to-high vigor rootstocks at low-to-medium densities, but intensive systems select self-compatible cultivars for effective pollination and dwarfing rootstocks for higher densities</cite>. 
- Rootstock choice is a first-order agronomic lever: growth-controlling dwarfing rootstocks enable “super high-density” systems with narrow rows and compact canopies that mature earlier, increase cropping frequency, and improve labor/mechanization efficiency—key to achieving high area productivity and expansion <cite id="e7009f37-0">Growth-controlling rootstocks enable super high-density systems with narrow rows/canopies, enhancing input efficiency and precocity</cite>. 
- In contrast, walnut and pistachio cultivation often accommodate multivoltine pests over longer, staggered vulnerability windows; management complexity and harvest timing differ, which can slow area expansion relative to almonds when pollination and harvest logistics are streamlined by cultivar/rootstock selection <cite id="ca57f832-3">Navel orangeworm affects California almond, pistachio, and walnut; new crop Nonpareil almonds are vulnerable for 5–8 weeks at harvest, and pistachios have an 8–10 week post-hull-split vulnerability period</cite>. 

5) Pest and disease management: shared risks and integrated control needs
- Almonds, pistachios, and walnuts share the navel orangeworm, a multivoltine moth with aflatoxin-producing fungal associates; this elevates the cost and complexity of season-long monitoring and integrated management, especially during extended preharvest dry-downs when nuts are most vulnerable <cite id="ca57f832-3">Navel orangeworm is primary pest across almond, pistachio, and walnut; monitoring is critical due to phenology-driven vulnerability windows and aflatoxin risk</cite>. 
- In practice, almond and pistachio orchards dry down for 13–14 days prior to harvest to synchronize shuckability; pest/disease risk management is time-sensitive and resource-intensive, but the economic value of high-value nuts supports these inputs and infrastructure, facilitating large-scale adoption in irrigated basins <cite id="ca57f832-2">Almond and pistachio orchards were dried for 14 and 13 days preharvest, respectively, as part of structured irrigation scheduling</cite>. 
- Compared with some other tree nuts, this shared pest complex and the need for tight agronomic scheduling are major drivers of input intensity; however, economies of scale in irrigation, pollination, and pest monitoring have allowed almond area to expand rapidly where markets and infrastructure exist <cite id="ca57f832-3">The combined farm gate value of these crops exceeds $9B in California (>900,000 ha), underscoring strong market and management support despite elevated pest/disease risks</cite>. 

6) Harvest logistics and processing: shorter, synchronized harvest windows and mechanization
- Almond varieties like Nonpareil have a concentrated 5–8 week harvest vulnerability and shuckability window after hull split, enabling synchronized orchard operations and efficient mechanical harvesting—logistics that align well with irrigation-intensive regions capable of rapid, repeated passes for thinning, irrigation control, and shaker-based harvest <cite id="ca57f832-3">Nonpareil almonds become vulnerable at hull split for 5–8 weeks until harvest</cite>. 
- Pistachio systems similarly schedule irrigation and implement 8–10 week vulnerability windows post-hull split, with preharvest drying for early October harvest; these practices illustrate that tree nut expansion depends on agronomic control of moisture and canopy to align with processing and market windows <cite id="ca57f832-2">Pistachio vulnerability follows hull breakdown for eight to ten weeks from mid-August through mid-October with structured irrigation and 13-day drying before harvest</cite>. 
- Orchards that can be dried down and shaken efficiently reduce labor per hectare relative to tree nuts with more fragmented harvest logistics, supporting higher area share when irrigation water and mechanization are available <cite id="ca57f832-2">Preharvest drying schedules and drip irrigation management demonstrate how irrigation timing directly controls harvest logistics</cite>. 

7) Market value and intensification: high value enabling efficient input use
- The global demand for almonds has expanded markedly in the past decade, driven by online channels and perceived health benefits; intensification pathways (precision irrigation, rootstocks, cultivars) convert less land into higher, more stable yields, reinforcing the economic logic of extensive planting where water and capital are available <cite id="e7009f37-2">Global demand growth from e-commerce and nutrition-driven markets has intensified almond cultivation, with intensive systems selecting cultivars and dwarfing rootstocks for higher yields and sustainability</cite>. 
- High-value crops support extensive research and extension to optimize cultivar/rootstock choices, irrigation scheduling, and pest monitoring; in California, >900,000 hectares of almonds, pistachios, and walnuts underpin a multi-billion dollar industry, showing how agronomic precision scales with economic value <cite id="ca57f832-3">California hosts >900,000 ha of almond, pistachio, and walnut with combined farm-gate value >$9B, highlighting the economic pull of high-value nut production</cite>. 

8) Comparative constraints vs other tree nuts
- Chestnuts and groundnuts tend to have lower overall water footprints per kg and protein, indicating agronomic niches where rainfall capture and lower input intensity are feasible, but they also face different processing/logistics and market dynamics that limit area share relative to almonds <cite id="fcb52f08-3">Chestnuts (9.7 L/g) and groundnuts (0.8 L/g) have much lower water footprints than almonds (65.4 L/kg) and others, reflecting different input and irrigation regimes</cite>. 
- Hazelnuts and walnuts often require higher chilling and have longer, staggered vulnerability periods and more complex canopy management; national programs invest in regional adaptation and logistics infrastructure to expand area, suggesting slower conversion to large-scale plantings compared with almonds where rootstock-driven intensification is mature <cite id="fcb52f08-0">Walnut and hazelnut area expansion in Ukraine is supported by associations focused on adaptation to local climatic conditions and logistics, reflecting longer-term, infrastructure-dependent growth</cite>. 
- Almonds also benefit from irrigation basins and export logistics tailored to their kernel traits; in contrast, nuts like pistachios and walnuts face higher aflatoxin risk during extended dry-downs and require robust monitoring, adding to management costs though not deterring area growth where inputs are available <cite id="ca57f832-3">Navel orangeworm and aflatoxin risk complicate almond, pistachio, and walnut management; economic value supports intensive monitoring and control</cite>. 
- Salinity and heat constraints remain a key agronomic boundary for almond expansion; unlike some tree nuts with broader salt tolerance, almond orchards often require water quality management and heat-stress mitigation (e.g., shade/deficit irrigation timing) to sustain yields in arid regions, which steers planting into irrigated corridors rather than dryland zones <cite id="e7009f37-2">Almonds’ poor salt-stress tolerance and sensitivity to high evaporative demand during fruit development drive targeted irrigation management and site selection</cite>. 

9) Synthesis: why almonds’ area share is disproportionate
- Almonds combine flexible but managed phenology, rootstock-enabled intensification, and irrigation-based climate control to deliver high yields per hectare where water and infrastructure exist, producing economies of scale in pollination, pest management, and mechanized harvest that are attractive to growers and investors <cite id="e7009f37-0">Rootstocks enabling super high-density systems improve input efficiency and precocity</cite><cite id="e7009f37-2">Dwarfing rootstocks, cultivar selection, and irrigation scheduling underpin intensive almond production</cite><cite id="ca57f832-2">Paired drip-irrigated almond and pistachio systems illustrate precise, scheduled water use and preharvest drying aligned to harvest</cite>. 
- Relative to many tree nuts, almonds’ concentrated harvest windows, kernel shuckability, and export logistics integrate well with irrigation-intensive regions, while their pest/disease risks are manageable at scale in high-value systems; these agronomic traits translate into high farm-gate value per hectare, reinforcing area expansion even where land and water compete with other crops <cite id="ca57f832-3">High-value almond, pistachio, and walnut systems justify intensive pest monitoring and drying schedules despite aflatoxin risks</cite><cite id="fcb52f08-3">Tree nuts show higher water footprints than groundnuts/chestnuts per gram, increasing the relative value of efficient irrigation and management</cite>. 
- Nonetheless, constraints—heat/water scarcity, salinity, and the need for continuous, metered irrigation—bound expansion to suitable basins; within those bounds, almonds’ superior ability to intensify (rootstocks, cultivars, mechanization) and their strong market demand explain their disproportionate 31% share of tree nut area <cite id="e7009f37-2">Prolonged water scarcity and high evaporative demand under poor salt tolerance severely compromise yields without careful irrigation and cultivar/rootstock selection</cite><cite id="e7009f37-0">Sustainability and intensification pathways in almond orchards focus on efficient labor and mechanization, enabling high productivity per hectare</cite>. 

10) Remaining uncertainties and what would resolve them
- Our comparison here emphasizes almonds, pistachios, walnuts, hazelnuts, and chestnuts; evidence gaps remain for macadamia (e.g., lethal yellowing), pecans (late blight/sudden death syndrome), cashews (cashew nut syndrome and aflatoxin), and Brazil nuts (low yields, canopy management, altitude). Targeted agronomic studies quantifying chilling requirements, rainfall dependence, irrigation footprints, and pest/disease burdens across these species, and regional irrigation infrastructure cost/availability (e.g., Central Valley vs India/Pakistan basins) would sharpen the attribution of area shares to agronomic drivers. 
</answer>

Title: Architectural approach to evaluate the design and management of almond cultivars suitable for super high-density orchards
Snippet: The almond tree (Prunus amygdalus (L.) Batsch = P. dulcis (Mill.)) is a dominant global tree nut crop, accounting for 31% of total nut crop production and with 700 thousand hectares planted worldwide (Iglesias and Torrents, 2022). Its production has risen substantially worldwide, increasing by 60% in the last ten years (USDA, 2024). The almond tree is widespread throughout the Mediterranean basin and is part of the agricultural biodiversity and food production systems, especially in Italy and Spain (Fernańdez i Martı́et al., 2009;Socias i Company et al., 2009;Alhajj Ali et al., 2023). Sustainability and efficiency are key factors in new agriculture, in which every cultivation technique must be innovated to improve the soil-plant-environment system and the efficient use of the input (e.g. irrigation water management and fertilizers) (Morugań-Coronado et al., 2020;Garofalo et al., 2024). A shift in cropping systems toward Sustainable Intensification (SI) pathways is imperative. SI is broadly defined as increasing agricultural production on existing land, reducing environmental impacts, and enhancing the provision of environmental services (Cano et al., 2023;FAO, 2024). The demand for innovation in fruit tree cultivation has led to the development of highly efficient and sustainable planting systems that move beyond the traditional open vase tree shape, already studied and applied to other species, such as olive, in which intensification from low to Super High-density (SHD) presented the greatest improvements, both for yield and Net Ecosystem Productivity (Mairech et al., 2020). These new agronomic models for almond production focus on growthcontrolling rootstocks, enabling orchard intensification with narrow rows and canopies, thereby enhancing input efficiency, particularly labor and mechanization, while promoting orchard precocity (Ghelfi and Palmieri, 2015;Iglesias et al., 2021;Maldera et al., 2023).

Title: Almond Tree Adaptation to Water Stress: Differences in Physiological Performance and Yield Responses among Four Cultivar Grown in Mediterranean Environment
Snippet: The growing global market demand has much contributed to this cultural intensification, prompted by the affirmation of the web market and by consumer recognition of the high nutritional and nutraceutical value of almonds [10]. Despite the biodiversity of almond varieties in the Mediterranean basin [2,3,11], today, almond production is dominated by a few commercial varieties [12]. In Italy, only a few local varieties are still cultivated, while 329 cultivar are referred and characterized (about 140 varieties in Apulia, 100 in Sicily, 40 in Sardinia, and 13 in Abruzzo). In addition, most Italian almond orchards are planted with self-incompatible and early-blooming varieties, exploiting a variety of gametophytic compatibility for cross-pollination [6,13]. Usually, these orchards are grown using the traditional systems, grafted onto rootstocks of medium to high vigor, with low to medium planting densities [14], unirrigated, or applying emergency and low re-watering supplies with drip irrigation [7,15]. 

The key to success in the new intensive almond orchards was strongly supported by the selection of blooming and self-compatible cultivar, to guarantee effective pollination, with low susceptibility to chlorosis and higher resistance to pests and diseases. In addition, the selection of new dwarfing rootstocks, with greater tolerance to asphyxia and chlorosis, enabled higher planting densities [16]. However, to ensure high yields and economic sustainability of such plants, the use of low-deficit irrigation strategies during periods of greatest water needs and scarcity becomes essential [17][18][19]. Furthermore, the impact of ongoing global warming challenges the sustainability and survival of new intensive cropping systems [17,20]. Despite almond's drought resistance, it has poor salt stress tolerance [21,22], and prolonged water scarcity during fruit developmental stages, concomitant with high atmospheric evaporative demand, severely compromises annual yields [23,24]. In Mediterranean arid or semi-arid climates, seasonal drought combined with heat waves and limited irrigation supplies result in a rapid decline in plant water status.

Title: The special place of walnuts in the world market and their transportation (case study of Uzbekistan)
Snippet: From the figure, three cultures can be distinguished -pistachios, almonds, and walnuts [3]. On the world market such varieties of nuts as pistachios, almonds, walnuts are in great demand. Pistachios give harvest in industrial quantities for the third year, but bringing them to the commodity kind, is quite a complex process. Leaders in the cultivation of pistachios in the world market for a long time are Iran, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, it is difficult to compete with them. That's why Uzbekistan has chosen a different nut culture [4]. 

Due to the great demand for walnut crops all over the world, a complex of logistics and transportation is developing. In Uzbekistan, in support of walnut production, on June 1, 2017, the Association of Walnut Producers and Exporters was established. The objectives of the association are the development of walnut growing in the Republic of Uzbekistan, the increase in the production of walnuts, almonds, pistachios, which can compete not only in the domestic but also in the world market. 

Another important task is the coordination of the implementation of plans for creating plantations of walnuts, almonds and pistachios in a modern style, the formation and conduct of various research works on adapting walnut, almonds and pistachios seedlings to territorial climatic conditions [5]. 

The Association of Walnut Producers and Exporters in the Republic of Uzbekistan consists of: LLC Scientific Research Center for Nut Growing. It conducts research on the acclimatization and regionalization of problematic varieties of walnuts, almonds and pistachios. 

Walnut Logistics Center LLC. The purpose of this organization is to provide services for the processing and storage of nut products, and to assist in the preparation of customs clearance of products for export. 

LLC MTP Sag agro. It provides services for agricultural events, producers, processors of walnuts, almonds, pistachios. 

Territorial divisions of Engokargo. It provides all types of services and interests of the Association in each region of the Republic of Uzbekistan.

Title: Monitoring Crop Evapotranspiration and Crop Coefficients over an Almond and Pistachio Orchard Throughout Remote Sensing
Snippet: The irrigation system consisted on two drip lines of eight drippers per tree with a discharge rate of 3.8 L•h −1 . The amount of irrigation water applied in the almond and pistachio orchards during the growing season was 898.0 and 762.5 mm, respectively. Irrigation in both orchards was scheduled following the protocol of the nut company. The almond orchard was irrigated weekly with a timing ranging from 2 (beginning of the season) to 70 hours/week (after harvest of cv. Nonpareil). From August through mid-September, the almond orchard was dried for periods of 14 days to enable harvest. In pistachio, irrigation periods ranged from 5 (beginning of the season) to 50 hours•week −1 (late July) and the orchard was dried for a period of 13 days before harvest (early October).

Title: Season-long comparison of trap lures for integrated management of the navel orangeworm (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae) in almond and pistachio
Snippet: The navel orangeworm, Amyelois transitella Walker (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae) is the primary pest of California almond (Prunus dulcis; 81% of the world supply), pistachio (Pistacia vera; 67% of the world supply) and walnut (Juglans regia) (Statista 2022, Almonds 2023). Currently these crops are planted in > 900,000 ha in California and have a combined annual farm gate value exceeding US $9 billion (Siegel and Gilcrease 2022). This multivoltine moth has a mutualistic relationship with fungal species belonging to the genus Aspergillus that produce aflatoxins, consequently feeding causes direct damage to the nuts and can cause secondary fungal infection (Palumbo et al. 2014;Ampt et al. 2016;Picot et al. 2017;Bush et al. 2018). 

Monitoring for A. transitella is important because damage in almonds and pistachios results from a complex interplay of crop phenology and pest population dynamics (Wilson et al. 2020). New crop Nonpareil almonds, the most valuable variety, become vulnerable during hull split (late June-July) when the suture widens exposing the shell and/or nut. The period of vulnerability for Nonpareil almonds typically lasts 5 to 8 weeks until the nuts are shaken from the tree at harvest; the other almond varieties mature from late August through October (Haviland et al. 2022a). New crop pistachios are vulnerable when the hull breaks down after the nut ripens, exposing the split shell for eight to ten weeks from mid-August through mid-October (Haviland et al. 2022b).

snippet.text:
The navel orangeworm, Amyelois transitella Walker (Lepidoptera: Pyralidae) is the primary pest of California almond (Prunus dulcis; 81% of the world supply), pistachio (Pistacia vera; 67% of the world supply) and walnut (Juglans regia) (Statista 2022, Almonds 2023). Currently these crops are planted in > 900,000 ha in California and have a combined annual farm gate value exceeding US $9 billion (Siegel and Gilcrease 2022). This multivoltine moth has a mutualistic relationship with fungal species belonging to the genus Aspergillus that produce aflatoxins, consequently feeding causes direct damage to the nuts and can cause secondary fungal infection (Palumbo et al. 2014;Ampt et al. 2016;Picot et al. 2017;Bush et al. 2018). 

Monitoring for A. transitella is important because damage in almonds and pistachios results from a complex interplay of crop phenology and pest population dynamics (Wilson et al. 2020). New crop Nonpareil almonds, the most valuable variety, become vulnerable during hull split (late June-July) when the suture widens exposing the shell and/or nut. The period of vulnerability for Nonpareil almonds typically lasts 5 to 8 weeks until the nuts are shaken from the tree at harvest; the other almond varieties mature from late August through October (Haviland et al. 2022a). New crop pistachios are vulnerable when the hull breaks down after the nut ripens, exposing the split shell for eight to ten weeks from mid-August through mid-October (Haviland et al. 2022b).

Title: Enterprise Activity Modeling in Walnut Sector in Ukraine
Snippet: In the context of global climate change and through new trends in the agri-food market, over the past two decades, there has been a tangible increase in the demand for the production and consumption of nuts. Official data testifies to the relevance of growing nuts. Thus, according to the annual report of the International Nut and Dried Fruit Council Foundation (INC) over the past 10 years, global nut production has grown steadily and in the 2019/20 financial year amounted to 4,600,000 t [1]. 

The main types of nuts include the so-called "Big Five": walnuts, almonds, pistachios, cashews and hazelnuts. In terms of harvest, almonds and walnuts are the leaders, accounting for 31% and 21% of world production, respectively, followed by cashews (17%), pistachios (14%) and hazelnuts (12%). The remaining 5% comes from the production of pecans, macadamias, Brazil nuts, and pine nuts [2]. 

Currently, walnut production in Ukraine is a profitable type of entrepreneurial activity at the level of farms, which appeared to be a systematic business in the country during the last years. The area of industrial walnut plantations in Ukraine is growing dynamically every year. According to the data of the Ukrainian Walnut Association, the most annual growth of walnut plantations in Ukraine falls on the creation of industrial hazelnut orchards and is more than 1000-1400 ha annually. The actual area of planted gardens in 2020 is about 3000 ha. Thus, in the central Ukraine region, there are a number of small farms that grow walnuts on 10-15 ha of land and perform their primary processing. Hence, since 2015 hundreds of hectares of modern, intensive gardens of walnuts and hazelnuts were planted using the technologies of inter-row planting until the garden reaches its estimated capacity. According to the International Nuts and Dried Fruit Council Foundation [1] the cost of the processed raw materials, i.e., walnut kernels, intended for further use in the agro-food chain, varies in the European market from 4 to 9 EUR/kg.

Snippet: Groundnuts (214 L/kg) and chestnuts (174 L/kg) show considerable smaller WFs.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer completely fails to identify the numerical impossibility in the premise. It accepts and repeatedly cites both the 700,000 ha figure and the 31% area share as simultaneously true throughout the entire response. The answer never questions whether these numbers are compatible with global tree nut production data.
